title: The derivative and the mean value theorem proved
objectives: Prove Rolle’s theorem and the mean value theorem from the definition of the derivative.

screens.title: A corner at 0
screens.prose: The derivative at 0 would be the limit of $\tfrac{f(h) - f(0)}{h}$ as $h \to 0$. Here $f(x) = |x|$. The dashed line joins $(0, 0)$ to P; its slope is the quotient. Drag P to the right of 0, then close in.

screens.question: What is the quotient for every $h > 0$?

hints.text: So the quotient is $\tfrac{h}{h}$.
It is 1, however small $h$ is.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $|h| = h$ when $h > 0$.

byKey.minus: That is the left side, $h < 0$, where $|h| = -h$. Keep P to the right.
byKey.zero: You read the height at 0. The quotient is a slope, $\tfrac{|h|}{h}$, and it stays 1.

explain.text: For $h > 0$ the quotient is $\tfrac{h}{h} = 1$, so its right-hand limit is 1. The dashed line keeps slope 1 as P slides in. Now try the other side.

screens.title: The other side
screens.prose: Now drag P to the left of 0 and close in again.

derive.caption: $h$ = {{fixed(P.x, 2)}}: the quotient $\tfrac{f(h) - f(0)}{h}$ is {{abs(P.x) < 0.005 ? 'undefined at h = 0' : fixed(abs(P.x) / P.x, 2)}}.

screens.question: What is the quotient for every $h < 0$?

hints.text: So the quotient is $\tfrac{-h}{h}$.
It is $-1$ for every $h < 0$.

feedback.correct: Right. $-1$ on the left, 1 on the right.

byKey.plus: You kept $|h| = h$. For $h < 0$, $|h| = -h$, so the quotient is $-1$.
byKey.zero: You read the height. The slope of the dashed line is $-1$.

explain.text: The one-sided limits are $-1$ and 1. They differ, so the quotient has no limit at 0. So $|x|$ has no derivative at 0.

screens.title: The derivative as a limit
screens.prose: $f$ is **differentiable at $a$** when $$f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$$ exists. The limit is in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ sense of l15, from both sides at once.
screens.question: Is $|x|$ differentiable at 0?

options.text: No: the quotient is $-1$ on the left and 1 on the right, so it has no limit.
Yes, with $f'(0) = 0$, the average of $-1$ and 1.
options.why: You averaged the one-sided limits. A limit needs both sides to agree; averaging invents a value.

options.text: Yes, because $|x|$ is continuous at 0.
options.why: You took continuity for differentiability. $|x|$ is continuous at 0, yet its quotient has no limit there.

options.text: Yes, $f'(0) = 1$, from the right.
options.why: You kept one side. The definition needs the limit from both sides.

hints.text: A limit exists only when both sides agree.
The left quotients are $-1$, the right ones 1.
They disagree, so no limit.

feedback.correct: Right. No derivative at the corner.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two one-sided limits you found.

explain.text: Within any $\delta$ of 0 the quotient takes both values $-1$ and 1. So for $\varepsilon = \tfrac12$ no single number $L$ works. The corner has no derivative, though $|x|$ is continuous there.

screens.title: Differentiable implies continuous
screens.prose: The converse does hold: differentiable at $a$ implies continuous at $a$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: For $x \ne a$, write $f(x) - f(a) = \dfrac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} \cdot (x - a)$.
As $x \to a$, the quotient tends to $f'(a)$ and $x - a$ tends to 0.
By the product law for limits, $f(x) - f(a) \to f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0$.
Since $f$ is continuous, the quotient converges to $f'(a)$.
lines.why: You argued the converse. Continuity does not make the quotient converge: $|x|$ at 0.

hints.text: Multiply and divide by $x - a$.
Then take limits of the two factors.
Order: rewrite, two limits, product law, conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. A finite slope times a vanishing step is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rewrite $f(x) - f(a)$ as a product, then use the product law.

byKey.d1: You used continuity to get the derivative. That direction is false, as $|x|$ shows.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The quotient has a finite limit and the step $x - a$ shrinks to 0. Their product tends to 0, so $f(x) \to f(a)$. Every differentiable function is continuous, but not conversely.

screens.title: Right of a maximum
screens.prose: $f$ has a maximum at $c = 1$, inside the interval. Drag P to the right of $c$. The dashed line from the top to P has slope $\tfrac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$.

derive.caption: $x$ = {{fixed(P.x, 2)}}: $\tfrac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ = {{abs(P.x - 1) < 0.005 ? 'undefined at x = c' : fixed(1 - P.x, 2)}}.

screens.question: For $x > c$, what sign does the quotient have, and why?

options.text: $\le 0$: $f(x) - f(c) \le 0$ at a maximum, and $x - c > 0$.
$\ge 0$: the graph rose to reach the top.
options.why: You read the climb on the left. To the right of $c$ the curve is at or below the top, while $x - c > 0$.

options.text: $= 0$: the tangent at the top is flat.
options.why: You used the conclusion. Each quotient is a secant slope, and to the right of $c$ it is negative here.

options.text: Either sign, depending on $x$.
options.why: You forgot what a maximum gives: $f(x) \le f(c)$ for every $x$. With $x > c$ the sign is fixed.

hints.text: At a maximum, $f(x) \le f(c)$ for every $x$.
So the top of the quotient is $\le 0$, and the bottom $x - c$ is positive.
A non-positive number over a positive one is $\le 0$.

feedback.correct: Right. Every right quotient is $\le 0$, so its limit $f'(c) \le 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the signs of $f(x) - f(c)$ and of $x - c$ separately.

explain.text: For $x > c$: $f(x) - f(c) \le 0$ and $x - c > 0$, so the quotient is $\le 0$. Limits keep $\le$, so $f'(c) \le 0$. The other side will give the reverse.

screens.title: Left of a maximum
screens.prose: Now drag P to the left of $c$.

derive.caption: $x$ = {{fixed(P.x, 2)}}: $\tfrac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ = {{abs(P.x - 1) < 0.005 ? 'undefined at x = c' : fixed(1 - P.x, 2)}}.

screens.question: For $x < c$, what sign does the quotient have?

options.text: $\le 0$, as on the right.
options.why: You kept the right-hand sign. Now $x - c < 0$, and a non-positive number over a negative one is $\ge 0$.

options.text: $= 0$, since the curve is near the top.
options.why: Near is not equal. The secant from the top to P slopes upwards to the right, so its slope is positive.

options.text: $< 0$, since P is below the top.
options.why: You read only the numerator. The denominator $x - c$ is negative too.

hints.text: $f(x) - f(c) \le 0$ still.
Now $x - c < 0$.
Dividing a number $\le 0$ by a negative number gives a number $\ge 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the sign of $x - c$ when $x < c$.

explain.text: Left quotients are $\ge 0$, so $f'(c) \ge 0$; right quotients gave $f'(c) \le 0$. If $f'(c)$ exists, both hold. So $f'(c) = 0$.

screens.title: The interior extremum theorem
screens.prose: Prove: if $f$ has a maximum at an interior point $c$ of $(a, b)$ and $f'(c)$ exists, then $f'(c) = 0$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Since $c$ is a maximum, $f(x) - f(c) \le 0$ for every $x \in (a, b)$.
For $x > c$ the quotient $\tfrac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ is $\le 0$, so its limit gives $f'(c) \le 0$.
For $x < c$ the quotient is $\ge 0$, so its limit gives $f'(c) \ge 0$.
The graph looks flat at the top, so $f'(c) = 0$.
lines.why: A picture is not a proof. The flat look is what the sign argument proves.
You argued the converse. $x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$ and no maximum at 0.

hints.text: Start from what a maximum gives: $f(x) \le f(c)$.
Then the two sides; they may come in either order.
Two inequalities on $f'(c)$ pin it to 0.

feedback.correct: Right. $\le 0$ from the right, $\ge 0$ from the left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f(x) \le f(c)$, then the sign of the quotient on each side.

byKey.d1: You used a picture. The proof must show the slope is 0, from the definition.
byKey.d2: You used the converse. A zero derivative does not make a maximum.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: A maximum makes every numerator $\le 0$. The denominators change sign across $c$, so the one-sided limits are $\le 0$ and $\ge 0$. Interior matters: at an end point only one side exists.

screens.title: Rolle's theorem proved
screens.prose: Rolle: if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$, then $f'(c) = 0$ for some $c \in (a, b)$. `limits` l17 used it; now we prove it. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: By the extreme value theorem (l17), $f$ attains a maximum $M$ and a minimum $m$ on $[a, b]$.
If both are attained only at the end points, then $M = m$ since $f(a) = f(b)$. So $f$ is constant and $f' = 0$ throughout.
Otherwise one of them is attained at some $c$ in $(a, b)$.
$f$ is differentiable at $c$, so by the interior extremum theorem $f'(c) = 0$. $\blacksquare$
The graph rises and then falls, so it has a flat top.
lines.why: You described a picture. Some functions with $f(a) = f(b)$ fall first, and a picture proves nothing.

hints.text: Which theorem gives a maximum and a minimum?
Split into the case where both sit at the ends and the case where one is inside.
Inside, use the interior extremum theorem.

feedback.correct: Right. The extremes exist; if they are both at the ends, $f$ is constant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Get the extremes from l17, then split on where they are attained.

byKey.d1: You used a picture. The proof uses the extreme value theorem instead.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The extreme value theorem gives the extremes. If both are at the ends they are equal, so $f$ is constant. Otherwise one is interior, and the interior extremum theorem gives $f'(c) = 0$.

screens.title: What each hypothesis did
screens.prose: Look back at the proof of Rolle's theorem.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which hypotheses did the proof use?

options.text: $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, for the extreme value theorem.
$f$ is differentiable on $(a, b)$, for the interior extremum theorem.
$f(a) = f(b)$, to make $f$ constant when both extremes are at the ends.
$f$ is differentiable at $a$ and $b$.
options.why: The proof never used a derivative at the ends. $\sqrt{x(1 - x)}$ on $[0, 1]$ has none there, and Rolle still holds.

options.text: $f'$ is continuous on $(a, b)$.
options.why: The proof used $f'(c)$ only at one point. Continuity of $f'$ is never needed.

hints.text: Go through the proof line by line.
Line 1 needs continuity, the last line needs a derivative at $c$.
The constant case needs the ends to agree.

feedback.correct: Right. Three hypotheses, each used once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each line of the proof, name the hypothesis it needs.

explain.text: Continuity on $[a, b]$ gives the extremes, $f(a) = f(b)$ settles the end case, and differentiability inside gives $f'(c) = 0$. Nothing is needed at the ends or of $f'$ itself. Drop any of the three and $|x|$ or a jump breaks it.

screens.title: Tilting Rolle
screens.prose: For the mean value theorem, subtract the chord: $$g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}(x - a).$$ Then $g(a) = g(b) = 0$, so Rolle applies to $g$. Take $f(x) = x^2$ on $[1, 3]$.
screens.question: Write $g(x)$ for $f(x) = x^2$ on $[1, 3]$, multiplied out.

hints.text: $f(a) = 1$, $f(b) = 9$, and the chord slope is $\tfrac{9 - 1}{3 - 1} = 4$.
Multiply out: $x^2 - 1 - 4x + 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f(a) = 1$ and slope 4: $g(x) = x^2 - 1 - 4(x - 1)$.

byKey.noline: You subtracted $f(a)$ but not the chord. Subtract $4(x - 1)$ as well.
byKey.slope: You used slope 8, the rise without dividing by the run 2. The chord slope is 4.

explain.text: $g(x) = (x - 1)(x - 3)$, so $g(1) = g(3) = 0$. Rolle gives $g'(c) = 2c - 4 = 0$, so $c = 2$. There $f'(2) = 4$, the chord slope.

screens.title: Flat but not a top
screens.prose: A classmate turns the theorem round: wherever $f'(c) = 0$, $f$ has a maximum or a minimum. Test it on $f(x) = x^3$ at 0, where $f'(0) = 0$.
screens.question: Does $x^3$ have a maximum or a minimum at 0?

options.text: Neither: $x^3 < 0$ just left of 0 and $x^3 > 0$ just right.
A minimum, since $f'(0) = 0$ and $0^3 = 0$.
options.why: You used the converse. Just left of 0, $x^3 < 0 = f(0)$, so 0 is not a minimum.

options.text: A maximum, since the tangent is flat.
options.why: You trusted the flat tangent. Just right of 0, $x^3 > 0 = f(0)$.

options.text: Both, since the curve is flat on each side.
options.why: The curve is not flat on either side: $f'(x) = 3x^2 > 0$ for $x \ne 0$.

hints.text: Compare $f(x)$ with $f(0) = 0$ on each side.
One side is below, one above.

feedback.correct: Right. A flat tangent does not make an extreme.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at values of $x^3$ on both sides of 0.

byKey.min: You read $f'(0) = 0$ as proof of an extreme. The theorem runs one way: extreme implies flat, not flat implies extreme.

explain.text: $x^3$ is below 0 on the left and above on the right, so 0 is neither. The theorem says interior extremes are flat, not that flat points are extremes. Flat points are only candidates.

screens.title: A call spread priced too wide
screens.prose: A call price $C(K)$ falls as the strike $K$ rises, with $-1 \le C'(K) \le 0$. By the mean value theorem, $|C(100) - C(105)| \le 5$. The market quotes the 100 call at £8.00 and the 105 call at £2.50.
screens.question: Sell the 100 call and buy the 105 call. What profit is locked in, at least?

widget.accept: £0.50: collect £5.50, and the payout is at most £5.

hints.text: Selling the 100 call brings in £8.00; buying the 105 call costs £2.50.
At expiry you owe $\max(S - 100, 0) - \max(S - 105, 0)$, which is between 0 and 5.
So the profit is at least $5.50 - 5$.

feedback.correct: Right. At least £0.50, whatever the stock does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the cash collected and subtract the largest possible payout.

byKey.gross: You counted the cash collected. At expiry you may owe up to £5 back.
byKey.bound: That is the most you can owe. The profit is the £5.50 collected minus it.
byKey.sum: You added the two premiums. You receive one and pay the other.

explain.text: The mean value theorem gives $C(100) - C(105) = -C'(\xi) \times 5 \le 5$ for some $\xi$. Quotes £5.50 apart break that bound. Selling the spread for £5.50 against a payout of at most £5 locks in at least £0.50.

ideas: $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \tfrac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$. Differentiable implies continuous; $|x|$ at 0, with one-sided quotients $-1$ and 1, shows the converse fails.
At an interior maximum the right quotients are $\le 0$ and the left ones $\ge 0$, so $f'(c) = 0$. With the extreme value theorem this proves Rolle.
Mean value theorem: Rolle applied to $g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \tfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}(x - a)$. So $|f'| \le M$ gives $|f(x) - f(y)| \le M|x - y|$.

formula.name: Mean value theorem
formula.note: For some $c$ in $(a, b)$. For $x^2$ on $[1, 3]$, $g(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$ and $c = 2$.

summary.trap: Flat does not mean extreme: $x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$ and no maximum or minimum at 0. And a flat-looking picture is not a proof.

quiz.prose: Take $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 3]$. The chord slope is $\tfrac{27 - 0}{3 - 0} = 9$.
quiz.question: Find $c \in (0, 3)$ with $f'(c) = 9$. Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $3c^2 = 9$ for $c$ in $(0, 3)$.

byKey.mid: You took the midpoint. There $f'(1.5) = 6.75$, not 9.
byKey.slope: You gave the slope, 9. The question asks where the tangent has that slope.
byKey.three: You solved $c^2 = 9$. The derivative is $3c^2$, so $c^2 = 3$.

explain.text: $f'(c) = 3c^2 = 9$ gives $c^2 = 3$, so $c = \sqrt 3 \approx 1.732$. It lies in $(0, 3)$, as the theorem promised. It is not the midpoint 1.5.

quiz.question: What does the mean value theorem give for any $x$ and $y$?

options.why: You treated the bound as the slope. The theorem gives $f'(\xi)$ for some $\xi$, and $|f'(\xi)| \le 2$ only bounds it.

options.text: $|f(x)| \le 2$ for every $x$.
options.why: You bounded the values. A slope bound limits change, not size: $f(x) = 2x$ is unbounded.
You squared the step. The change is the slope times the step, to the first power.

feedback.correct: Right. A slope bound is a bound on change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $f(x) - f(y) = f'(\xi)(x - y)$ and bound $f'(\xi)$.

explain.text: The theorem gives $f(x) - f(y) = f'(\xi)(x - y)$ for some $\xi$ between them. Taking sizes, $|f(x) - f(y)| \le 2|x - y|$. With bound 0, every $f(x) = f(y)$, so $f$ is constant.

options.text: $f'(0) = 0$, since the quotient $x\sin(\tfrac1x) \to 0$; but $f'$ is not continuous at 0.
$f'(0)$ does not exist, since $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ oscillates.
options.why: You stopped at the oscillation. The quotient is $x\sin(\tfrac1x)$, squeezed to 0 as in l15.
You assumed $f'$ is continuous. $-\cos(\tfrac1x)$ keeps swinging between $-1$ and 1.

options.text: $f'(0)$ is the formula's value at 0.
options.why: The formula has $\tfrac1x$ in it, so it says nothing at 0. Use the quotient.

feedback.correct: Right. Differentiable everywhere, yet $f'$ jumps about at 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $f'(0)$ from the quotient, then ask whether $f'(x)$ has a limit.

explain.text: $\tfrac{f(x) - f(0)}{x} = x\sin(\tfrac1x)$, and $|x\sin(\tfrac1x)| \le |x| \to 0$, so $f'(0) = 0$. But $f'(x)$ contains $-\cos(\tfrac1x)$, which has no limit. A derivative can exist everywhere and still be discontinuous.

quiz.prose: $f'(x) = 0$ for every $x$ in an interval $I$. To show $f$ is constant, take $x < y$ in $I$.
quiz.question: Which step finishes the proof?

options.text: The mean value theorem on $[x, y]$: $f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x) = 0$.
Rolle on $[x, y]$ gives $f(x) = f(y)$.
options.why: You ran Rolle backwards. Rolle assumes $f(x) = f(y)$; it cannot prove it.

options.text: $f$ has no slope, so its graph is a horizontal line.
options.why: You described the picture. The proof must connect $f'$ to values, which the mean value theorem does.

options.text: $f$ is continuous, so it is constant.
options.why: Continuity alone allows $f(x) = x$. The zero derivative is what forces constancy.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Connect $f(y) - f(x)$ to a derivative value.

explain.text: For any $x < y$ in $I$, the theorem gives $c$ with $f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x) = 0$. So every two values agree, and $f$ is constant. On two separate intervals this fails, as a step function shows.
